title: What were war masks?
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore World War One facial disfigurement and the "war masks" made to restore soldiers' appearance. They cover the wartime rise in facial wounds from machine guns and shrapnel, early plastic surgery history (Sushruta's rhinoplasty, syphilis-related facial destruction, skin grafting), and Sir Harold Gillies's hospital at Sidcup. They then describe Francis Derwent Wood's Masks for Facial Disfigurement Department (the "Tin Noses" shop) and Anna Coleman Ladd's Paris studio, how the copper portrait masks were made from plaster casts and squeezes and hand-painted to match skin tone, their short lifespan and the fact that few survive, and the postwar social stigma faced by disfigured veterans. The episode ends with a listener mail about a president Franklin Pierce descendant.

segments.title: Intro and WWI facial wounds
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the hidden history of facial disfigurement in World War One, explaining that machine guns and shrapnel from mortar shells caused new kinds of facial wounds while improved battlefield medicine let more soldiers survive them.

segments.title: History of early plastic surgery
segments.summary: The hosts review early plastic surgery, including an Indian doctor's rhinoplasty technique from about 500 BC, nose punishment for theft, syphilis-caused facial destruction, and eighteenth and nineteenth century skin grafting, before WWI pushed reconstructive surgery forward.

segments.title: Gillies at Sidcup and surgical limits
segments.summary: Sir Harold Gillies ran a hospital at Sidcup outside London where British soldiers underwent a series of reconstructive surgeries. When surgery reached its limits, patients were sent to Francis Derwent Wood and Anna Coleman Ladd. The hosts describe skin flap techniques and Gillies's book on plastic surgery of the face.

segments.title: Social stigma and blue benches
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how society shunned disfigured veterans, including blue-painted benches warning the public near Sidcup and the absence of mirrors in hospitals, and reflect on changing attitudes toward facial differences.

segments.title: Derwent Wood and the Tin Noses shop
segments.summary: Francis Derwent Wood, an artist who enlisted at age forty-four, founded the Masks for Facial Disfigurement Department, nicknamed the Tin Noses shop by soldiers. He made portrait masks restoring identity rather than function. Kathleen Scott praised the men's dignity, and the department was established in March 1916.

segments.title: Anna Coleman Ladd's Paris studio
segments.summary: American sculptor Anna Coleman Ladd, whose husband Maynard Ladd was a physician with the Red Cross, set up a Studio for Portrait Masks in Paris's Latin Quarter, a bright, flower-filled space. Newsreel footage shows her fitting a mask on a patient.

segments.title: How the masks were made and their fate
segments.summary: The masks were made from plaster casts, clay squeezes, and copper about a playing card's thickness, with real hair for mustaches and enamel paint matched to skin tone. Masks lasted a couple of years, were attached by spectacles or over the ears, and few survive since many were buried with owners. Ladd made about 185 masks; Wood made more. Ladd and Wood died young, and postwar veterans faced isolation.

segments.title: Listener mail: Franklin Pierce relative
segments.summary: A listener named Sarah, mother of a Pierce, writes that her husband is a great-great-nephew of President Franklin Pierce and that the family considers him one of the worst presidents. The hosts respond.
